src: U.S. Energy Information Administration, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (public domain); positions written by hand for Global Intelligence Atlas

rows.name: STRAIT OF HORMUZ
rows.description: Links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The EIA calls it the world's most important oil chokepoint.

rows.name: STRAIT OF MALACCA
rows.description: Between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra: the shortest sea route between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, linking Middle Eastern and African suppliers with Asian markets.

rows.name: SUEZ CANAL
rows.description: Connects the Red Sea and the Mediterranean; together with the SUMED pipeline beside it, the main route for oil and gas from the Persian Gulf to Europe.

rows.name: BAB EL-MANDEB
rows.description: Between Yemen and Djibouti and Eritrea, joining the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Ships bound for the Suez Canal pass through it.

rows.name: TURKISH STRAITS
rows.description: The Bosporus and the Dardanelles, through Istanbul: the only sea route from the Black Sea and its oil ports to the Mediterranean.

rows.name: DANISH STRAITS
rows.description: The Øresund and the Great and Little Belts between Denmark and Sweden: the route from Baltic ports, including Russia's, to the North Sea.

rows.name: PANAMA CANAL
rows.description: Joins the Atlantic and Pacific across Panama; its locks limit the size of ships, and droughts that lower Gatun Lake limit how many can pass.

rows.name: CAPE OF GOOD HOPE
rows.description: Not a strait but the long way round Africa, which tankers take when the Suez Canal or Bab el-Mandeb is closed or too dangerous.
